title: To know one another
hook: We made you nations and tribes to know one another, and the most honored is the most mindful (49:13)
carry: made different to know each other

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was ghibah, backbiting, true or not, and your line was not behind their back. When a conversation turned to someone absent, what did you do? Day five hundred eighty-eight, the end of the week.

Stand in the courtyard of the Great Mosque of Mecca during the pilgrimage and listen. Arabic, Urdu, Malay, Turkish, Swahili, Hausa, Bosnian, French, English with a Texas accent. Faces of every shade. Two million people, give or take, in the same white cloth. Ask most of them for one verse about why humanity looks like this, and many will give you the same one. It's the thirteenth verse of Surah Al-Hujurat, and it's addressed not to believers this time, but to everyone.

Notice the shift. Every command in this surah so far began: O ye who believe. Verse thirteen opens wider. Pickthall's translation: "O mankind! Lo! We have created you male and female, and have made you nations and tribes that ye may know one another. Lo! the noblest of you, in the sight of Allah, is the best in conduct." Three moves. First, one origin: male and female, which commentators read as Adam and Hawwa, one family. Second, deliberate difference: nations and tribes, made, on purpose. Third, the purpose of that difference, in one Arabic word: li-ta'arafu, so that you may know one another. The form of the verb means mutual knowing, back and forth, each side learning the other. Its root is the same as ma'ruf, the known good, and 'urf, custom. Difference here isn't a problem to solve. It's an introduction. And then the ranking is taken away from everything you can see. The noblest is the most mindful; the Arabic is atqakum, from taqwa, the awareness of God. Not the richest, not the oldest family, not the right tribe. And taqwa can't be seen from outside. Only Allah knows who has it. A sermon attributed to the Prophet ﷺ during his farewell pilgrimage, recorded in the Musnad of Ahmad, put it plainly: no Arab has merit over a non-Arab, nor a non-Arab over an Arab, nor white over black, nor black over white, except by taqwa. This week has been the surah's whole lesson in talking well: a pledge, a lower voice, checked news, peace made, mocking dropped, backbiting refused. It ends here, with why the people across the table are different in the first place.
screen: `O MANKIND: THE VERSE OPENS WIDER.` · `ONE ORIGIN, DELIBERATE DIFFERENCE.` · `LI-TA'ARAFU: KNOWING EACH OTHER.` · `THE NOBLEST: THE MOST MINDFUL.`

segments.voice: The practice: learn one thing about another culture. Sit, and breathe. Picture someone you see often whose background is different from yours: a neighbor, a coworker, the person who runs the shop on the corner. Think about what you actually know about where they come from. Probably not much. Choose one question you could ask them kindly this week: a food, a holiday, a word in their language. If you pray, you can thank Allah for the variety of people. The bell holds the time.
To know one another. Li-ta'arafu: the purpose 49:13 gives for nations and tribes, mutual knowing, with nobility measured only by taqwa. Today's word.
Your line: made different to know each other. Today, ask one person from a different background one real question, and listen to the whole answer. Day five hundred eighty-eight.

howItsDone: Muslims often cite 49:13 against racism and tribalism, and the farewell sermon's words on Arab and non-Arab, black and white, are widely read in Friday sermons and at the pilgrimage.

fork.reveal: li-ta'arafu: difference made on purpose, for mutual knowing; nobility only by taqwa.

original.note: Arabic: so that you may know one another (49:13); root '-r-f, as in ma'ruf.

trapdoor: what you thought: a nice line about diversity.
what it means: one origin, deliberate difference, a purpose of mutual knowing, and nobility only by taqwa, which no one can see.
what a scholar hears: ta'aruf is a mutual verb form from '-r-f, the root of ma'ruf; the farewell sermon in Musnad Ahmad applies it to Arab and non-Arab, black and white.
